title: Wild helpers in the field
text: In one study of mustard and sunflower farms, researchers counted the insects that visited flowers each day. Honeybees were the most numerous visitors, but they were far from the only ones. Solitary bees, hoverflies and even beetles also carried pollen from plant to plant. Honeybees tended to work the same few plants again and again, which limited how far pollen travelled. Wild visitors moved more erratically, and this wandering helped to mix pollen from many different plants. The fields with the greatest variety of insects produced the heaviest seed crops, even where the number of honeybee hives was the same. The researchers do not suggest that beekeeping should be abandoned. Their point is that farmers who clear hedgerows and spray flowering margins may be removing the very helpers that raise their yields. Leaving a strip of wild flowers beside the crop costs little land, and it gives wild insects food and shelter between harvests.

stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Honeybees are poor pollinators and should be replaced by wild insects.
Mustard and sunflower crops cannot be grown without hedgerows.
Wild insects contribute to crop pollination, so farms should protect their habitat.
Farmers should spray flowering margins to attract more beetles.
explanation: The passage reports that wild insects add to pollination and that habitat strips help them; it does not call honeybees poor pollinators, nor does it recommend spraying.

stem: According to the passage, why did honeybees limit the distance pollen travelled?
options: They flew only on days when the beetles and hoverflies were absent from the fields.
They avoided the mustard flowers altogether and visited only sunflower plants.
They were too few in number to cover all of the fields in the study.
They kept returning to the same few plants again and again.
explanation: The text says honeybees were numerous but worked the same few plants repeatedly. Their numbers were not the problem.

stem: The word 'erratically' in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: unpredictably
slowly
quietly
carefully
explanation: Wild visitors wandered from plant to plant without a fixed pattern, which is what 'unpredictably' conveys; nothing suggests they moved slowly or carefully.

stem: Which fields produced the heaviest seed crops?
options: Those with the largest number of honeybee hives
Those visited by the widest variety of insects
Those with no hedgerows beside the crop at all
Those sprayed most often along the flowering margins
explanation: The passage states that variety of insects, not the number of hives, went with the heaviest crops.

stem: Which of the following would the author most likely agree with?
options: Beekeeping should stop wherever wild insects are already present in the fields.
Wild insects matter only on very small farms with few honeybee hives.

Beekeeping and wild-flower strips can both be useful to a farmer.
explanation: The author explicitly says beekeeping need not be abandoned while recommending habitat for wild insects, so both are useful.

stem: What can be inferred about a wild-flower strip beside a crop?
options: It will replace honeybees completely once it has been sown.
It is expensive because it takes up so much of the farmland.
It attracts only beetles and no other kind of insect visitor.
It may raise yields indirectly by sustaining wild insects.
explanation: The strip costs little land and gives insects food and shelter, which supports the helpers that raise yields. The passage does not say it replaces honeybees.

title: Streets of an ancient city
text: The ruins of Mohenjo-daro, in Sindh, show that its builders cared a great deal about everyday cleanliness. Many houses had a bathing area, and waste water ran from it into small drains built of baked brick. These joined larger covered drains that ran beneath the main streets, and removable bricks allowed workers to clear blockages. A visitor today can still trace these channels in the brickwork. Such planning suggests more than skill with bricks. It suggests that someone organised the work, that households were expected to follow common rules, and that the drains were maintained after they were built. A drain is useful only if it is kept clear, and the long life of these structures points to regular care. Archaeologists are careful, however, about guessing how the city was governed. The drains tell us what people built, not who gave the orders. Other questions, such as who lived in each house, must be answered by different kinds of evidence.

stem: What is the main point of the passage?
options: The drainage system of Mohenjo-daro points to careful planning and upkeep.
Mohenjo-daro was governed by a single powerful ruler.
Baked brick was used only for drains in Sindh.
Archaeologists have solved every question about the city.
explanation: The passage uses the drains as evidence of planning and maintenance, but it warns that they do not reveal who ruled.

stem: According to the passage, how could workers clear blockages in the large drains?
options: By flooding the streets with water until the drains cleared
By taking out bricks that were made to be removable
By breaking the drains open at the end of each season
By sending the waste back to the bathing areas
explanation: The passage says removable bricks allowed workers to clear blockages.

stem: The author says the drains suggest 'more than skill with bricks'. This means the drains also suggest
options: organisation and shared rules
a shortage of building material
a wish to hide waste from visitors to the city
the use of metal tools
explanation: The next sentences list organised work, common rules and maintenance as what the drains imply beyond bricklaying skill.

stem: Why does the author mention that 'a drain is useful only if it is kept clear'?
options: To show that the drains often failed in the years after they were built
To support the claim that the structures were regularly maintained
To explain why bathing areas were rare in the houses
To argue that the city was abandoned early
explanation: Their long life, together with the need to keep drains clear, is used as evidence of regular care.

stem: Which question does the passage say the drains cannot answer?
options: Whether the houses in the city had bathing areas
What kind of material the drains were made of
Who gave the orders to build them
Where the large drains were placed beneath the streets
explanation: The passage states that the drains tell us what people built, not who gave the orders.

stem: The tone of the passage is best described as
options: humorous and light
angry and critical
boastful and certain
careful and measured
explanation: The author draws sensible conclusions but warns against guessing about governance, which is a careful, measured stance.

title: The lending library
text: When the Nawaz family moved to a new neighbourhood in Lahore, their daughter Hira was unhappy about leaving her old school and friends. Her mother noticed a small lending library at the end of the street, run by retired teachers from a rented room. Members paid a small monthly fee and could borrow two books at a time. Hira joined reluctantly and chose a book of short stories only because the cover was bright. Within a month she was visiting twice a week. The librarians soon learned her taste and began leaving suitable books on a shelf for her. They also started a weekly reading hour, where children read aloud to one another. Hira's confidence grew, and so did her marks in English. The library never held many books and its furniture was old, but it offered something larger shelves cannot: people who knew what each reader needed. Her mother later said that the fee was the best money the family had ever spent.

options: Why libraries should charge higher fees
A teacher's retirement plans
The decline of old schools
How a small library helped a lonely girl
explanation: The passage follows Hira from reluctant member to confident reader thanks to the library's people.

stem: How many books could a member borrow at one time?
options: Two
One
Three
Five
explanation: The passage says members could borrow two books at a time.

stem: Why did Hira choose her first book?

It was the shortest book in the room.
explanation: The text says she chose the short stories only because the cover was bright.

stem: The word 'reluctantly' in the passage most nearly means
options: happily
unwillingly

explanation: She was unhappy about the move and joined without enthusiasm, which is what 'unwillingly' means.

options: Newer furniture and more space for readers
Cheaper membership than any of the schools

explanation: The final sentences state that the library offered people who knew what each reader needed.

explanation: The author contrasts a small collection and old furniture with the librarians' attention; the other options are not supported.

title: Why prices rise
text: Inflation is often described as a rise in the general level of prices, but its effects are felt unevenly. A family that spends most of its income on food and fuel notices price rises at once, because it cannot easily cut back on either. A wealthier family may barely notice, as a smaller share of its income goes on necessities. Savers are also affected. If a bank pays four per cent a year and prices rise by seven per cent, the money in the account buys less each year, even though the balance is growing. Borrowers can sometimes gain, since the sum they repay is worth less than the sum they received. Economists therefore do not treat inflation as simply good or bad. A slow, steady rise lets businesses and households plan ahead. Rapid and unpredictable rises make planning difficult, because nobody knows what a contract signed today will be worth next year. It is this uncertainty, more than the rise itself, that most worries policymakers.

stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Inflation always benefits borrowers and harms savers.
Wealthy families are the only ones harmed by rising prices.
Banks should never pay interest on savings.
Inflation affects different people differently, and unpredictable inflation is the larger concern.
explanation: The passage shows uneven effects and says uncertainty worries policymakers most. 'Always' is too strong because borrowers 'sometimes' gain.

stem: According to the passage, why does a family that spends most of its income on food and fuel notice inflation quickly?
options: It cannot easily reduce its spending on those items.
It earns less interest on its savings than richer families do.
It borrows more heavily than wealthier families do.
It buys most of its goods from abroad.
explanation: The passage says such a family cannot easily cut back on food or fuel.

stem: In the bank example, what happens to the saver's money?
options: It buys more each year as the balance grows.
It loses value only because the bank charges high fees each year.
It buys less each year although the balance grows.
It stays equal in value to the original sum.
explanation: With interest at four per cent and prices up seven per cent, purchasing power falls even while the balance rises.

stem: Why can borrowers sometimes gain from inflation?
options: The money they repay is worth less than the money they received.
Banks lower the loan amount automatically.
Their wages stop rising.
Prices of necessities fall.
explanation: As prices rise, a fixed repayment is worth less in real terms than the sum borrowed.

stem: Which statement best describes the author's view of a slow, steady rise in prices?
options: It is more harmful than rapid and unpredictable inflation.
It allows households and businesses to plan ahead.
It helps only wealthy families and no one else.
It removes the need for contracts between businesses.
explanation: The passage says slow and steady rises let people plan ahead; unpredictable rises are the real difficulty.

stem: As used in the passage, 'uncertainty' refers to
options: not knowing what money will be worth in the future
a lack of banks in the economy
disagreement among economists about how to define inflation
a fall in the price of food
explanation: The author ties uncertainty to nobody knowing what a contract signed today will be worth next year.

title: Forests on the shoreline
text: Mangrove trees grow where few other trees can: in salty mud that is flooded twice a day by the tide. Their roots rise above the surface and form a dense tangle, which slows moving water and lets fine mud settle. Over many years this process can build up new land. The tangle of roots also shelters young fish, crabs and prawns, so fishing communities near mangroves often depend on them without realising it. In addition, a wide belt of mangroves can weaken waves during storms, protecting villages behind it. Despite these benefits, mangroves have often been cut for fuel or cleared to make way for shrimp ponds and building plots. Replanting is possible, but it works best when the right species are placed at the right height in the tide, and many early projects failed because the seedlings were planted too low and drowned. Success usually needs the cooperation of local people, who understand the shore better than any visiting planner.

stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How to build shrimp ponds on a coast
Why storms occur along the shore
The value of mangroves and the need to protect and replant them carefully
The history of fishing villages
explanation: The passage describes benefits, threats and careful replanting of mangroves.

stem: How do mangrove roots help build new land?
options: They slow water so that fine mud settles.
They draw salt out of the soil around them.
They break rocks on the shore into fine sand.
They prevent the tide from rising at all.
explanation: The text says the dense roots slow moving water and let fine mud settle, which can build land over time.

stem: Why do fishing communities benefit from mangroves?
options: Mangroves produce fuel for the boats that go out to fish.
Mangroves keep the water in the creeks fresh.
The roots shelter young fish, crabs and prawns.
The trees attract large ships to the fishing villages.
explanation: The roots shelter young sea animals which later feed local fisheries.

stem: According to the passage, why did many early replanting projects fail?
options: The seedlings were planted in fresh water.
Seedlings were planted too low in the tide and drowned.
Local people refused to take part.
Storms uprooted all the seedlings.
explanation: The passage states seedlings were planted too low and drowned.

stem: The phrase 'without realising it' suggests that fishing communities
options: dislike mangroves because the trees block their boats
are completely unaware that any mangroves grow on their coast
pay money each year to protect the mangroves nearby
benefit from mangroves although they may not notice it
explanation: The communities depend on mangroves for fish stocks, yet may not connect the two.

stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the final sentence?
options: Visiting planners should be avoided entirely in every project.
Replanting should never be attempted along a muddy shore.
Only fishing communities can plant trees along a coast.
Local knowledge is important for successful replanting.
explanation: The author says success usually needs local cooperation because people know the shore best. 'Avoided entirely' is too strong.

title: Money on the phone
text: A decade ago, many families in small towns had to travel to a bank branch to send money to relatives. The journey cost time and fare, and the queue could be long. Mobile payment services have changed this routine. A shopkeeper now acts as an agent who takes cash and sends a message to the recipient, who collects the amount at another agent nearby or keeps it in a phone account. For households that never had a bank account, this has been a first step into the financial system. The services have their own risks, however. Fraudsters send false messages claiming that money was sent by mistake and ask for it back. Users who share their secret number with a stranger can lose their balance in minutes. Agents may also run out of cash on busy days. Companies and regulators therefore spend considerable effort on teaching users simple habits: never reveal the secret number, check the amount before confirming, and keep receipts. Convenience, it seems, works best when users are careful.

options: Banks no longer exist in small towns because of mobile payment agents.
Fraud has made mobile payments useless for most households.
Mobile payments have made sending money easier but require careful use.
Agents should be replaced by branches because of the risk of fraud.
explanation: The passage describes convenience and the risks, ending with the need for care.

options: They receive free mobile phones.

explanation: The passage says it is a first step into the financial system for such households.

explanation: The text says agents may run out of cash on busy days.

explanation: The passage lists never revealing the secret number, checking the amount and keeping receipts.

options: the agent who sends the money on the sender's behalf
the regulator who checks the services each month
the company that owns the phone network

explanation: The recipient collects the amount at another agent or keeps it in a phone account, so it is the receiver.

options: The benefits of the service can be lost through careless behaviour.

explanation: The author says convenience works best when users are careful, implying carelessness reduces its benefits.

title: The beauty of the written word
text: Calligraphy is the art of making writing beautiful, and it has long been honoured in the Muslim world, partly because it joined two things people valued: the written word and visual design. A calligrapher spends years learning how to cut a reed pen, mix ink and form each letter with the correct proportions. Even a short line may be written many times before it satisfies the artist. Different scripts developed for different uses. Some are upright and clear, suited to copying long texts; others are flowing and decorative, used for titles and for panels on buildings. Learning the rules does not mean copying without thought. Great calligraphers are remembered because they combined strict training with a personal sense of rhythm, so that the same letters look unmistakably theirs. Today computers can produce neat lettering in seconds, yet handwritten calligraphy continues to attract students. Many say that the slow, steady practice teaches patience, and that no machine can reproduce the small variations that give a hand-written page its warmth.

explanation: The passage discusses training, scripts and continued appeal; pen cutting is only a detail.

explanation: The text says great calligraphers combined strict training with a personal sense of rhythm.

explanation: The upright and clear scripts are described as suited to copying long texts.

explanation: The same letters look clearly the artist's own, so 'recognisably' fits.

title: Sleep and learning
text: Students who stay up all night before an examination believe they are using their time well, yet studies of sleep suggest otherwise. During sleep, the brain does not simply switch off. It appears to replay the events of the day and to strengthen the links that matter, which helps new facts to become lasting memories. People who learn a list of words and then sleep generally recall more of it the next day than people who learn it and stay awake for the same number of hours. Sleep also affects attention. A tired person makes more careless errors and finds it harder to follow a long argument. None of this means that revision is worthless. Facts must be learned before they can be stored. The sensible approach is to study in shorter periods over several days and keep a regular bedtime. A student who does so arrives at the examination with knowledge that has had time to settle, and with a mind able to use it.

stem: What is the main message of the passage?
options: Revision is worthless if done before sleep.

Sleep helps memory and attention, so staying up all night to study is unwise.
The brain stops working during sleep.
explanation: The passage argues sleep supports learning, but revision itself remains necessary.

stem: According to the passage, what happens to the brain during sleep?
options: It switches off completely and stores nothing at all until the person wakes.
It appears to replay the day's events and strengthen important links.
It forgets recent facts to make space for new ones.
It stops forming memories but repairs the body.
explanation: The passage says the brain does not switch off, but replays events and strengthens links.

explanation: The comparison shows sleepers recall more.

explanation: The final part recommends shorter periods across days and a regular bedtime.

title: Words that travelled
text: Before the fifteenth century, books in Europe were copied by hand, and a single volume could take months to finish. Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg, working in Mainz, combined movable metal type with a press and an oil-based ink, and printing in Europe changed quickly. A printer could now produce hundreds of identical pages from letters that were arranged, used and then rearranged. Books became cheaper, and more people had reason to learn to read. Printing did not create new ideas by itself, but it allowed them to spread faster than before. A pamphlet written in one city could be reprinted in another within weeks. Authorities sometimes tried to control what was printed, which shows that they understood its power. Historians still debate how large the effect was in each country, because literacy grew slowly and unevenly. What is not in doubt is that texts were no longer rare objects kept in a few libraries. Knowledge had begun to travel in a form that many people could own.

stem: Which statement best summarises the passage?
options: Gutenberg invented the idea of reading, and ordinary people in Europe followed.
Printing ended all official control over books in every country.
Europe had no books at all before the year 1450.

explanation: The passage presents printing as a means for faster, cheaper spread of texts, not as the creator of ideas or the end of control.

explanation: The first sentence says books were copied by hand, taking months.

stem: What could a printer do with movable type?
options: Use each set of letters only once

explanation: The text says letters were arranged, used and then rearranged.

options: They disliked paper because it was brought from abroad.

explanation: Efforts at control 'show that they understood its power'.

explanation: The passage gives uneven growth of literacy as the reason.

stem: The phrase 'what is not in doubt' introduces a statement that the author
options: regards as certain

explanation: The phrase marks a point that is accepted: texts were no longer rare objects.

title: Cycling to work
text: City planners often argue about whether new cycle lanes are worth their cost. Critics point out that few commuters cycle in cities where roads are crowded and unsafe, and conclude that lanes would go unused. Supporters reply that the lack of cyclists is the result of danger, not of unwillingness. When a protected lane is built, they say, people who never considered a bicycle begin to try it. Evidence from a number of cities shows that the number of cyclists often rises after a lane opens, although the rise depends on whether the lane links useful places. A lane that stops abruptly at a busy junction is little better than none. Cycling also has benefits that are not obvious from traffic counts. A bicycle takes up little road space, produces no fumes and costs a fraction of a car to run. It follows that even a modest shift from cars may ease congestion and household budgets alike. The real question is not whether lanes cost money but whether they are built where they will be used.

Cycle lanes pay off when they are safe and built where people will use them.
Cars should be banned from cities so that cycling becomes safe.
Commuters dislike cycling for no reason that planners can understand.
explanation: The passage weighs both sides and concludes with the importance of location and safety.

explanation: Supporters say the lack of cyclists results from danger, not unwillingness.

stem: According to the passage, what makes a lane 'little better than none'?
options: It stops suddenly at a busy junction.
It is painted in bright colours.

explanation: The text says a lane that stops abruptly at a busy junction is little better than none.

explanation: A lane that ends 'abruptly' ends suddenly, leaving riders at the junction.

stem: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a benefit of bicycles?

stem: What does the final sentence suggest about the debate on cycle lanes?

title: Why we trade
text: Imagine two villages, one beside a river and one among hills. People in the first village can catch fish easily but find it hard to raise sheep, while those in the hills can do the opposite. If each village tries to produce everything for itself, both spend long hours on tasks they do badly. If instead each concentrates on what it does best and trades the surplus, both can have more fish and more wool than before. This idea, called specialisation, lies behind much of the world's trade. It does not require one village to be better at everything; even a village that is slower at both tasks gains by concentrating on the one at which it is less poor. The arrangement is not free of risk, however. A village that depends on a single product suffers if its price falls or if the buyers stop coming. For this reason, successful traders usually specialise while keeping a few other skills in reserve. The lesson of the two villages is that exchange can make both sides better off.

stem: What is the main point of the passage?
options: Villages should avoid all trade.
One village must be better at everything to trade.
Fish is more valuable than wool.
Specialisation and trade can leave both sides better off, though it carries some risk.
explanation: The passage explains benefits of specialisation and then its main risk.

stem: According to the passage, what happens if each village tries to produce everything for itself?
options: Both produce much more than they need for themselves.
Both spend long hours on tasks they do badly.
Neither can catch fish in the river.
Both stop using the hills and the river.
explanation: The passage says both would spend long hours on tasks they do badly.

stem: What is the risk of depending on a single product?
options: The product can no longer be exchanged with other villages.
Specialisation becomes illegal in neighbouring villages.
A fall in price or loss of buyers can hurt the village.
Workers forget how to farm after a few seasons.
explanation: The text says the village suffers if the price falls or buyers stop coming.

stem: Which statement does the passage support?
options: Only the fastest village gains from trade.
Trade works only between equal villages.
A village slower at both tasks can still gain from trade.
Specialisation removes all risk.
explanation: The passage says that even a village slower at both gains by concentrating on the task at which it is less poor.

stem: The word 'surplus' in the passage means
options: a shortage of goods that forces a village to trade
a type of tax paid on goods that cross a border
what is left over after one's own needs are met
the price at which a product is finally sold
explanation: Each village trades the part of its produce that it does not need itself.

stem: What can be inferred about 'successful traders'?
options: They balance specialisation with a few reserve skills.

title: Catching the rain
text: In many dry regions, rain arrives in a few heavy showers and then vanishes, running off roofs and roads before anyone can use it. Rainwater harvesting is a simple response: gutters lead the water from a roof into a tank or into a pit where it can soak into the ground. A household with a modest roof can collect many thousands of litres during a single wet season, enough to wash clothes and water a garden for months. Such water is not always safe to drink without treatment, because dust and bird droppings wash down with it, but it is suitable for many other tasks, which reduces pressure on the mains supply. Cities that require new buildings to include a tank have found that the burden on drains during storms also falls. The method is no cure for a serious drought, since a tank cannot fill when no rain falls. Its value lies in making the best use of the rain that does come, and in encouraging people to think of water as a resource to be saved rather than simply spent.

title: Storing the sun
text: Solar panels produce electricity only when the sun shines, but people want to use power at night as well. The usual solution is a battery, which stores energy during the day and releases it later. Batteries have improved greatly, yet they remain expensive and heavy for their size, and they lose capacity slowly as they age. A household that buys one must weigh these costs against the convenience. Some engineers favour other ways to store energy, such as pumping water up to a high tank by day and letting it run down through a turbine at night. This works well where there are hills and spare water, but not on a flat plain. Others point out that energy can be saved simply by using machines when the sun is out, running a water pump at noon rather than at dusk. No single method suits every place. The best plan usually mixes several, chosen according to local conditions, cost and the habits of those who will use the power.

title: Songs without a page
text: For centuries, many village songs were never written down. They passed from one singer to the next, usually learned in childhood at weddings and harvest gatherings. Because each singer remembered the song a little differently, versions of the same tune could vary from valley to valley. This was not carelessness. Singers changed words to suit the occasion, added a verse about a local event or dropped one that no longer made sense, and so the song stayed alive. When collectors began to record such songs on tape, they faced a difficult choice. A recording preserves one performance exactly, but it can make the song seem fixed, as if that single version were the correct one. Some collectors therefore recorded the same song from several singers and kept all the versions. Others worry that people may begin to copy the recording instead of singing from memory, and that the habit of change will fade. The question is not whether to record, since lost songs cannot be recovered, but how to record without freezing a living tradition.

title: When medicines stop working
text: Antibiotics are drugs that kill bacteria or stop them from multiplying. They do not work against viruses, so they are no use for a common cold. Bacteria in a large population are not all identical, and a few may by chance be able to survive a particular drug. If the drug is used often, the weaker bacteria die and the tougher ones multiply in their place, so that the next infection may be harder to treat. This is how resistance arises. It is made worse when people take antibiotics for illnesses they cannot cure, or use them without a doctor's advice. Doctors now try to prescribe antibiotics only when they are needed and to explain how they should be taken. Scientists are also searching for new drugs, but the process takes years. In the meantime the most practical defence is careful use: antibiotics are a limited resource, and every unnecessary dose makes the drugs a little less reliable for the person who truly needs them.

title: The road of silk and more
text: The name 'Silk Road' suggests a single highway, but it was in fact a network of routes crossing deserts, mountains and plains between China and lands to the west. Few merchants travelled the whole distance. Goods were passed from trader to trader, each of whom sold at a profit to the next, so a bale of silk might change hands many times before it reached its final buyer. Silk was only one of the goods carried. Spices, paper, glass, horses and metalwork also moved along the routes, as did ideas, religious beliefs and crafts. Cities that sat at the meeting points of routes, such as Samarkand and Kashgar, grew rich as markets and as places to rest. Travel was slow and often dangerous, and caravans paid fees to rulers whose lands they crossed. Historians use the term cautiously now, because it can hide how varied the trade was. Even so, the picture of goods and ideas passing along linked routes remains a useful way to understand how distant peoples influenced one another.

title: Giving time
text: Many charities rely on volunteers, and the usual view is that volunteers help others at their own cost. That is true, but it is only half of the picture. People who give their time regularly often report that they gain something in return. A retired clerk who teaches arithmetic to children after school may find that he feels useful again. A student who helps in a hospital reception may learn how to speak calmly to frightened people, a skill that no classroom lesson quite teaches. Volunteering also brings together people who would not otherwise meet, from different ages and backgrounds, and so builds the sort of trust that makes a neighbourhood function. None of this should be used as an excuse to treat volunteers as free labour. Organisations that value them train them, give them clear tasks and thank them sincerely. When a volunteer is left without guidance, the experience can be frustrating for everyone. Giving time works best when it is a fair exchange of effort and respect on both sides.

title: Shade in the city
text: On a hot afternoon, the temperature on a paved street in a city can be several degrees higher than in a nearby park. Concrete and asphalt soak up sunlight during the day and give the heat back slowly after dark, so that crowded districts stay warm long into the night. Trees reduce this effect in two ways. Their leaves cast shade, which keeps the ground cooler, and they release water vapour, which cools the air much as sweat cools skin. A row of mature trees along a road can make walking pleasant when the open street beyond is uncomfortable. Planting is not as simple as it sounds, however. Young trees need regular watering for several years, and the wrong species can damage pavements with their roots or drop heavy branches in storms. Councils that succeed usually choose local species suited to the soil and climate, and involve residents in looking after the saplings. The benefits, such as lower cooling costs and cleaner, more attractive streets, arrive slowly, but they last for decades.

title: Machines and jobs
text: Every wave of automation has produced the same fear: that machines will take work and leave people with nothing to do. History offers a mixed answer. When mechanical looms spread in the nineteenth century, many hand weavers lost their livelihoods, and the hardship was real. Yet cloth became cheaper, demand for it grew, and new jobs appeared in repairing machines, selling cloth and building factories. The overall number of jobs did not fall, although the jobs were different and not always offered to the same people. This is the point that careful observers stress. The question is not only whether work will exist but whether workers can move into it. A weaver of fifty cannot easily become a machine engineer. Training, savings to live on during a change, and support for those who must move can decide whether automation brings widespread benefit or widespread distress. Today's discussions about computers and robots echo the old ones. The lesson from the past is neither to welcome every machine without thought nor to resist all of them, but to prepare people for the change.

title: The neighbourhood kameti
text: In many Pakistani neighbourhoods, a group of ten neighbours agrees to put the same sum into a common pot each month. Each month one member takes the whole pot, and the order is fixed at the start, often by drawing lots. After ten months every member has paid in ten times and received the pot once. No interest is paid, and there is no bank. The arrangement works because the members trust one another, and because each knows that a member who failed to pay would lose the respect of the group. For a family that finds it hard to save a large sum alone, the system acts as a discipline. The money has already left the house before it can be spent on something else, and the pot arrives as a lump sum that can pay for a wedding, a machine or school fees. Its weakness is that the member who takes the pot last has lent to the others for months without reward, and a defaulter can damage the whole circle. Careful groups therefore choose their members with care.

title: Why the sea rises and falls
text: The regular rise and fall of the sea, known as the tide, is caused mainly by the pull of the Moon's gravity on the water of the Earth. The side of the Earth facing the Moon is pulled towards it, and the water there bulges outwards. Another bulge forms on the far side, so most coasts experience two high tides and two low tides in a little over a day. The Sun also pulls on the oceans, but because it is so much farther away its effect is smaller than the Moon's. When the Sun and Moon are lined up with the Earth, their pulls combine, and the tides are at their highest and lowest. When they are at right angles to each other, the tides are less extreme. The shape of the coast also matters. In a narrow bay the water is squeezed, and the tide can rise much higher than in the open sea. Sailors and fishermen have long relied on tide tables to plan their work, because arriving at a harbour at the wrong hour can leave a boat stranded on the mud.

title: The pleasure of reading
text: Some people say they have no time to read, yet many of them spend an hour each day looking at a phone. The difference is less about time than about habit. Putting a book aside when it fails to interest you is a sensible choice, not a failure. What matters is that reading becomes a regular and pleasant part of the day.

title: Letters across the land
text: Before telephones, the post was the way ordinary people kept in touch across distance, and a good postal system was one of the most valuable services a government could provide. The idea of a fixed charge for a letter, paid in advance by the sender with a stamp, was introduced in Britain in 1840 and soon copied elsewhere. Earlier, the receiver often paid on delivery, and many refused letters they could not afford. The prepaid stamp made posting simpler and faster, and the number of letters grew rapidly. Railways then carried mail over long distances far more quickly than coaches, and sorting could be done on the train itself. In places such as the Indian subcontinent, the post office reached remote villages and became a trusted public institution. People used it not only for letters but also to send money and to save small sums. Today messages travel in seconds, and few people write letters, yet the post still carries parcels and documents. Its history shows how a simple change, such as the stamp, can alter the habits of a whole society.
